To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have discovered three mutant forms of a multispanning membrane transport protein in yeast that are aberrantly retained in the endoplasmatic reticulum and that these mutants define at least two distinct classes of ER quality control.
we have identified a new class of ER retained Ste6p mutants and that the ER quality control pathway can be dissected into at least three distinct checkpoints.
we have identified three mutant versions of a yeast plasma membrane protein that are retained in the endoplasmatic reticulum and that two of these mutants define a linear ER quality control pathway.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the process of ER quality control, which is a critical aspect of protein folding in the cell.
the identification and characterization of ER quality control mechanisms in yeast.
the process of ER quality control and the identification of the components of this process in yeast.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have found that ER-retained Ste-6p mutants can be used as a tool to dissect the pathway for ER quality control.

we have identified a number of mutants of a multispanning membrane glycoprotein that define two distinct classes of aberrantly ER-retained forms, one of which is degraded via the ubiquitin-protesasome pathway, and that we have identified the proteasome sub-unit Hrd2p as a high-copy suppressor of the mating defect associated with one of these mutants.

the ER quality control mechanism in yeast appears to involve two distinct pathways: one that targets misfolded ER proteins for degradation and another that targets misfold proteins to a post-ER compartment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have identified a new ER quality control pathway that is involved in the degradation of aberrant Ste6p and that we have also identified a new role for the proteasome subunits Hrd1p and Hrd2p in the degradation of Ste6p.

the ER quality control pathway can be divided into two distinct steps: (a) a first checkpoint that involves the ubiquitin-dependent degradation of misfolded or unassembled proteins, and (b) a second checkpoint involving the proteasomal degradation of misfoldedd proteins in the ER membrane that have escaped the first checkpoint.

the ER quality control machinery in yeast has the capacity to distinguish among different classes of aberrantly folded multispanning membrane proteins and can channel them to different outcomes, including degradation and retention in the ER.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ER quality control in S. cerevisiae is not as simple as it was once thought to be.
ER quality control in the budding yeast is a more complex process than previously thought.
the yeast ER has evolved an elaborate quality control system to monitor the integrity and folding state of its membrane proteins.
